title: Are You a Should or Could Leader
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece examines the outsized difference between two small words leaders use when giving direction: 'should' and 'could.' Should functions as a command issued from a position of power, while could hands the decision back to the other person as a genuine option. The author shows how the same sentence lands very differently depending on which word is chosen, particularly when correcting a mistake. Most leaders default to should without noticing, even when their intent is to empower rather than direct. The piece closes by inviting readers to audit their own word choice as a lever for how much ownership they leave with others.
points: 'Should' is a directive issued from power; 'could' shares power and offers a genuine choice.
The same correction lands as a mandate or as a learning opportunity depending on the word used.
Most leaders default to 'should' out of habit, even when they intend to empower others.
Choosing 'could' more often signals whether an idea belongs to the leader or to the team member.
quotes: Using the word Should is not a request. It is an imperative demand, even if offered politely or with the intention of helping others.
When it comes to feedback, Could represents a sharing of power and changes the command to a suggestion to consider another option.
Directing people to do things differently invariably means dropping the Should bomb.
It is an imperative demand, even if offered politely or with the intention of helping others.
When leaders use the word Should , they do so from a place of power, expertise, or experience.
As such, they direct people to a different action or choice.
We empower others to make the call when we replace Should with C ould .

You should add another story to the presentation” has a very different implication than the statement, “You could add another story to the presentation.” The former statement is a directive, and may even be interpreted as a mandate or command.
